added.name: Creation and eternal life in Moses’ vision
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 1:27–39: Moses’ vision connects divine creation with human immortality and eternal life. A concept, not a place; nothing is drawn. See also: “Moses’ vision”.

added.name: Spiritual creation and the garden in Moses 3
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 3:1–25 joins spiritual creation, responsibility in the garden, choice and marital companionship. A concept; the garden is the existing Eden reference, not a new place. See also: “Garden in Eden”, “Creation in Moses”.

added.name: Rebellion before the garden narrative in Moses 4
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 4:1–4 and 12–31 present a rebellion against agency before the garden narrative, then its consequences and the expulsion. An ordered narrative with no numeric date. See also: “Leaving Eden in Moses”.

added.name: Cain’s line: Enoch to Lamech
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 5:41–53: Cain, then Enoch, Irad, Mahujael, Methusael and Lamech is this family branch. Lamech’s wives are Adah and Zillah; their children Jabal (tents and cattle), Jubal (music), Tubal Cain (metalworking) and Naamah supply the occupational and family context. The account says Lamech kills Irad after Irad begins revealing their secret, and Lamech’s wives then disclose it (verses 49–53). Irad keeps his place in the genealogy; no different victim is invented to remove the chronological difficulty. This Lamech, of Cain’s line, is not Noah’s father, and this Enoch is not the Enoch of Seth’s line. See also: “Cain in Nod”.

added.name: Seth’s line: Adam to Methuselah
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 6:2–25: Adam, then Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch and Methuselah is the other genealogy. Enos names a land for his son. Enoch’s movement by the sea east (verses 41–42) is a textual itinerary without geometry. Within Enoch’s discourse, Adam is described as being carried into water, baptized and born of the Spirit (verses 64–68): embedded speech about Adam, not Enoch’s baptism and not a located river. Cainan the person is not the land of Cainan, and this Enos is not the Book of Mormon writer. See also: “Land of Cainan”, “Enoch’s preaching”, “Enos and his people: Shulon to Cainan”.

added.name: Zion in Moses 7
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 7:18–21 gives the name Zion to a community with no poor among them and to its city; verses 62–69 promise a later gathering and a meeting with it. The ancient narrative and the future expectation are kept separate, and no place is drawn.

added.name: Lamech, Noah and Noah’s sons
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 8:5–13: Methuselah’s son Lamech fathers Noah, and Noah’s sons are named with distinct reported birth ages. The textual data are kept as given, not harmonized into dates. This Lamech is of Seth’s line, not Cain’s. See also: “Noah’s warning in Moses”.

added.name: Abraham, the priesthood records and Egyptian origins
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Abraham 1:7–12 and 15–31 link Abraham’s rescue and the priesthood records he inherited with an account of Egyptian origins. The three unnamed daughters of Onitah are killed after refusing idol worship. The text’s Egyptus and Pharaoh relationships stay source-specific: not every Pharaoh is collapsed into one ruler, and the Egyptus statements in verses 23 and 25 are not forced into a resolved family tree. A literary relationship, not established population history. See also: “Abraham’s deliverance”, “Facsimile 1: published explanation”.

added.name: Abraham’s covenant and household
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Abraham 2:1–11 and 14–25: the covenant concerns Abraham’s descendants and ministry to all families. He reports his brother Haran’s death, his own marriage to Sarai and his brother Nahor’s marriage to Milcah, Haran’s daughter. Lot and Lot’s unnamed wife travel from Ur; Terah follows but remains in Haran. Near Egypt, Abraham conveys an instruction that Sarai identify herself as his sister: reported speech, not independent evidence of biological kinship. The existing journey is reused; Terah is not moved through the entire path, and arrival in Egypt is not narrated as completed. See also: “Abraham’s narrated journey”.

added.name: Heavenly order and premortal intelligences
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Abraham 3:1–28: Abraham’s vision links heavenly ordering with premortal intelligences and a chosen mission. Not a scientific star map; nothing is drawn. See also: “Kolob”.

added.name: The Gods in counsel: Abraham’s creation account
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Abraham 4–5 uses plural divine actors and distinguishes counsel from formation. It is compared with the other accounts as its own account, not combined with them into one chronology. See also: “Creation in Abraham”, “Creation in Moses”.

added.name: Facsimile explanations as attributed interpretation
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — The explanations of all three facsimiles belong to the published scripture; their named figures and cosmic terms remain attributed interpretations. Published glosses are not independent Egyptian translations or measured astronomical bodies, and the evidence limit on the papyri still applies. See also: “Facsimile 1: published explanation”, “Facsimile 2: published explanation”, “Facsimile 3: published explanation”, “Book of Abraham: Church account of papyri”.

added.name: From the temple to the Mount of Olives
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—Matthew 1:2–4: Jesus goes from the temple to the Mount of Olives and there answers questions about the destruction and his coming. A two-place textual movement; no path is drawn. See also: “Prophecy in Joseph Smith—Matthew”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: family moves, marriage and translation
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:3–4 and 55–75: Joseph reports his birth at Sharon, Vermont; his father’s move from Vermont to Palmyra; and the family’s subsequent move to Manchester. He reports work in Harmony, marriage in South Bainbridge, return to his father’s farm and a move with Emma to Pennsylvania. Martin Harris separately takes characters to New York, and Joseph is not routed along Harris’s trip. Oliver Cowdery joins the translation before the reported baptism. These are a birthplace and reported migration episodes, not a complete direct Sharon–Palmyra route; the restoration places already in the atlas are reused. Verse 62’s December arrival context and the separate translation episodes are kept; April 7, 1829 is not asserted to be the beginning of all translation. Subranges: verses 1–4 frame and family; 5–13 inquiry; 14–20 vision; 21–26 opposition; 27–54 Moroni and the hill; 55–58 labor and marriage; 59–62 plates and move; 63–65 Harris; 66–67 Cowdery; 68–75 baptism and protection. Dates remain the account’s reported dates. See also: “Receiving the plates”.

added.name: Oliver Cowdery’s 1834 account, appended
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — The October 1834 reminiscence by Oliver Cowdery appended to Joseph Smith—History is a separate retrospective witness, not verse 76 and not part of Joseph’s narration.

added.name: The Church today on race and the priesthood
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — The Church’s current essay disavows explanations connecting Black skin to divine disfavor or premortal wrongdoing and rejects racial inferiority. It is shown with Moses 7:8 and 22 and Abraham 1:21–27, whose language is kept as written, not silently erased and not mapped onto modern ethnic groups. The essay is the Church’s current official position, not a rewritten ancient narrative. See also: “Racial priesthood and temple restrictions”.

src.t: Race and the Priesthood, “The Church Today”

added.name: Pearl of Great Price: publication dates
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — The official introduction: the collection appeared in 1851 and became a standard work on October 10, 1880; present Doctrine and Covenants sections 137 and 138 were added in 1976 and moved out in 1979. Document dates, not narrated ancient dates. See also: “Pearl of Great Price collection history”.

added.name: Articles of Faith 1–13, article by article
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Articles of Faith 1:1–13 is a confession of belief; it implies no dated journey or event. Article 1: belief in the Godhead. 2: individual accountability rather than Adam’s transgression. 3: Christ’s Atonement and salvation. 4: faith, repentance, baptism by immersion and laying on of hands. 5: calling and authority. 6: Church offices. 7: spiritual gifts. 8: the Bible with its translation qualification, and the Book of Mormon. 9: continuing revelation. 10: gathering, the New Jerusalem on the American continent and millennial hopes; no future footprint is drawn. 11: liberty of worship. 12: civic obligations. 13: ethical aspirations. Articles 1–3 are also in “Articles of Faith 1–3”, article 4 in “Principles and ordinances”, 5–7 in “Articles of Faith 5–7”, 8–9 in “Scripture and revelation”, and 10–13 in “Articles of Faith 10–13”.

before.name: Section 104: The firm divided into stewardships
before.desc: Doctrine and Covenants — Section 104. Dated April 23, 1834, at or near Kirtland. The United Firm is restructured into individual stewardships, with separate operations and treasuries in Ohio and Missouri. Stewardships: Sidney Rigdon, his residence and the tannery; Martin Harris, a lot involved in an exchange with John Johnson; Frederick G. Williams and Oliver Cowdery, the printing; John Johnson, his inheritance less reserved lots; Newel K. Whitney, houses, the store and the ashery; Joseph Smith, the temple lot of 40 by 12 rods and his father’s home. The sacred and general treasuries are separate. The April 10 decision and the April 23 direction are distinct, and the physical parcels need separate deeds before any mapping. See also: “The United Firm”, “Gathering, land and consecration”, “Bible revision, publication and records”, “Members of the United Firm”.

before.name: Section 124: Nauvoo: temple, house and offices
before.desc: Doctrine and Covenants — Section 124. Dated January 19, 1841, at Nauvoo, formerly Commerce. Distinct instructions for the Nauvoo temple, including proxy baptism, and for the Nauvoo House, a boarding house. A proclamation is to be written with Robert B. Thompson’s help and John C. Bennett’s labor, with Sidney Rigdon and William Law as further assistants. Nauvoo House trustees: George Miller, Lyman Wight, John Snider and Peter Haws; the president to be chosen among them is unnamed. Stock is set from $50 to $15,000; Joseph Smith Jr., Vinson Knight, Hyrum Smith, Isaac Galland, William Marks, Henry G. Sherwood, William Law, Amos Davies and Robert D. Foster are directed to subscribe, and Foster is instructed concerning building a house for Smith. Isaac Galland is to be ordained by William Marks and to go with Hyrum Smith, and a future mission of William Law with Hyrum is reserved; Law is to preach at Warsaw, Carthage, Burlington and Madison; Rigdon is to move near Smith, not east. Offices: Hyrum Smith, patriarch and seer; William Law replaces him as counselor; the Presidency of Joseph Smith with Sidney Rigdon and William Law. Brigham Young presides over the Twelve: Heber C. Kimball, Parley P. Pratt, Orson Pratt, Orson Hyde, William Smith, John Taylor, John E. Page, Wilford Woodruff, Willard Richards and George A. Smith, with the deceased David W. Patten noted; no twelfth living name is invented. High council: Samuel Bent, Henry G. Sherwood, George W. Harris, Charles C. Rich, Thomas Grover, Newel Knight, David Dort, Dunbar Wilson, Aaron Johnson (replacing the deceased Seymour Brunson), David Fullmer, Alpheus Cutler and William Huntington. High priests: Don C. Smith, president, with Amasa Lyman and Noah Packard. Elders: John A. Hicks, Samuel Williams and Jesse Baker. Seventy: Joseph Young, Josiah Butterfield, Daniel Miles, Henry Herriman, Zera Pulsipher, Levi W. Hancock and James Foster. Bishopric: Vinson Knight, Samuel H. Smith and Shadrach Roundy, Roundy “if he will receive it”; Samuel Rolfe presides over the priests. The deaths of David W. Patten, Edward Partridge, Joseph Smith Sr. and Seymour Brunson are remembered, and the oppressed builders of the Jackson County temple are excused, not shown as having completed it. Commanded appointments and construction are kept apart from their completion; ward presidents are unnamed, and household and property coordinates require historical sources. See also: “Nauvoo House”, “Nauvoo building and leadership instructions”, “Law’s regional preaching assignment”, “Offices, ordinances and discipline”, “Gathering, land and consecration”, “Bible revision, publication and records”, “Temple instructions”, “Family care, education and the poor”, “Joseph and Hyrum Smith: brothers with distinct offices”, “Offices named in section 124”.

before.name: Section 137: A vision including Alvin
before.desc: Doctrine and Covenants — Section 137. Dated January 21, 1836, at the Kirtland Temple. A vision including Alvin Smith: salvation beyond earthly knowledge, and children. Adam, Abraham, Joseph’s parents and Alvin are shown; those who would have received the gospel and children below the age of accountability are promised salvation. The vision includes parents then living; it is not a notice of deaths. It comes before section 109 in time, and the vision has no celestial or earthly coordinate. See also: “Bible revision, publication and records”, “Joseph Smith and his brother Alvin”.

after.desc: Doctrine and Covenants — Section 137. Dated January 21, 1836, at the Kirtland Temple. A vision including Joseph Smith’s brother Alvin: salvation beyond earthly knowledge, and children. before.name: Official Declaration 1: The Manifesto
before.desc: Doctrine and Covenants — Official Declaration 1. Wilford Woodruff’s statement, the Manifesto, is dated September 24, 1890, and was accepted on October 6, 1890, at a conference in Salt Lake City on Lorenzo Snow’s motion; the existing “Manifesto accepted” event is reused. The appended material includes an account of the Endowment House demolition and excerpts of addresses at Logan in 1891 and at the Salt Lake Temple in 1893, labelled as separate settings. The statement’s denials are read with the Church’s later acknowledgment of plural marriages after 1890; it was not an instantaneous end of all unions. See also: “Manifesto issued and explained”, “The Official Declarations: announcement and acceptance”, “Consent and command in section 132”, “Signatories and the motion to accept”.
